justification: Judged fresh before reopening the round-1/round-2 files. Every page that ranks for this query stops at one-line definitions plus a toy or analogy example: Microsoft Learn's tutorial extends a BankAccount with inherited account types and one virtual month-end method; freeCodeCamp uses four unrelated analogies (Printer, BankAccount, Animal, gift box) with no invariant discussion, no runtime mechanics, no cost discussion and no exercises; the broader search results (Medium, Scaler, AlmaBetter, Turing School, Pluralsight) are the same shape or thinner. This article's value-add is real and specific to each pillar: encapsulation as invariant protection with a broken-then-fixed Invoice program and an AsReadOnly leak exercise; a CoreCLR method-table figure tied to the Book of the Runtime plus a GetBaseDefinition reflection demo distinguishing override from `new`-hiding; overload resolution versus virtual dispatch; a delegate array as polymorphism with no inheritance at all; two runnable inheritance failure modes (a virtual call from a base constructor, an override breaking an unwritten postcondition) fixed with the Template Method pattern and then explicitly re-broken by a `new`-hiding SneakyPlan that shows the fix's guarantee is scoped to references typed as the base; and an abstraction section that argues what an interface should admit (Unreachable), not just that interfaces exist. Five exercises are spread through the article with collapsed solutions; none gives away its output before the solution. I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs` myself: PASS, blocks=29 executed=15. Copy check: four distinctive sentences searched in quotes ('who is able to put this object into a state that makes no sense', 'A good abstraction leaves out what varies between implementations', 'Encapsulation protects you from the first class onward', 'A rejected call leaves the invoice exactly as it was') returned no matching passage anywhere. Sourcing: 17 sources in front matter, every one cited at least once in the body (verified by counting each [[n]] marker), including the two added since round 2 - I re-fetched both: the Liskov and Wing 1994 PDF is at its canonical cs.cmu.edu location, and the C# 15 closed-hierarchies feature-spec page does describe a `closed` modifier that lets an exhaustive switch expression skip the fallback arm, matching the article's claim exactly. No filler intro or outro; the closing section argues which pillars to reach for first rather than repeating headings. Structure is not templated: heading set, openings and exercise titles (find the way in, predict what new does, move the check, extend the invariant, reason about a sealed call site) differ from the statement-heading siblings I compared (test-doubles.md, sql-joins.md, branching-and-merging.md); the question-heavy heading set matches the plan's assigned Q shape, not a site-wide tic. The 'X, not Y' contrast construction flagged in round 1 is gone except one ordinary list use ('frozen, not open, overpaid'). No keyword stuffing; title and description read as written for a human and accurately describe the depth (down to how .NET dispatches a virtual call). docs/crosslinks/oop-design/four-pillars-of-oop.md exists, is sensible, and still matches the current anchor sentences, so missing links to unpublished siblings are not an issue. Round-2 findings, checked against the current text: (1) Liskov and Wing 1994 - fixed: added to sources (entry 17, with URL and accessed date) and cited inline [[17]] at the sentence naming the principle, worded exactly as suggested ('known as the Liskov substitution principle; Liskov and Wing give its formal definition in...'). (2) Design Patterns / Gamma et al. citation looking like a citation for show - fixed: the publisher field now reads 'Addison-Wesley, 1994; publisher record, cited by chapter', which states plainly that the link is a bibliographic pointer, not the source of the chapter argument. (3) beginner level / empty prerequisites versus a page that reaches reflection and JIT devirtualization - not fixed. Front matter is unchanged from round 1 (level: beginner, prerequisites: []); the mitigations already in place (a plain definition at each pillar's first use, glosses of virtual/override/abstract at the Plan program, and the 'skip ahead... on a first read' signpost before the runtime-internals sections) are all still there and unchanged, so the practical harm to a true beginner is already contained, but the badge itself still overpromises. This is the same gap round 1 (major) and round 2 (minor, both adsense and design) found; it has now gone three rounds without a front-matter change, so it stays open. What keeps the score off a 10: that one persistent front-matter mismatch is the only nit left; everything else that a Google policy reviewer would hunt for - filler, padding, templating, near-duplicate coverage, copied or paraphrased passages, keyword stuffing, unsupported claims, invented experience or statistics, mass-produced boilerplate, dead-end navigation - is absent or has been closed since round 1.
